q: A provider's monthly report shows 500 tickets closed and 98% of them within target. The client says staff still lose hours every week to the same recurring fault. Which reading of the situation is most accurate?
opts: Outputs were delivered, but the outcome the client needed was not achieved
The outcome was achieved, since the agreed service levels were met
Neither outputs nor outcomes were achieved, since the fault keeps recurring
Outcomes were delivered, but the outputs fell short of the agreed service level
why: Closed tickets and target compliance are outputs: deliverables of the activity. The outcome the client needs, staff working without interruption, has not happened. Meeting service levels does not by itself prove the outcome was achieved, the outputs clearly were produced, and the claim that outcomes were delivered while outputs fell short reverses which half was delivered.

q: A cloud backup service has run at 99.99% availability for a year. When a restore is finally needed, the client discovers the service was never able to back up its Linux file servers, only its Windows ones. Which statement is most accurate?
opts: Warranty was adequate, but utility was lacking
Utility was adequate, but warranty was lacking
Both were adequate; the failure was purely an outcome problem
Neither was adequate, since a failed restore undermines availability
why: The service was available and reliable, so warranty (fit for use) was fine. It simply never did the thing the client needed, backing up Linux servers, which is a gap in utility (fit for purpose). Calling utility adequate and warranty lacking swaps the two; calling both adequate ignores the missing functionality; and calling neither adequate misreads a functional gap as an availability failure.

q: A department head negotiates the requirements for a new reporting service, funds it from her own cost centre, and never personally logs in to it. Which combination of roles does she hold?
opts: Customer and sponsor, but not user
Customer and user, but not sponsor
Sponsor only, since she does not use the service
Customer, user, and sponsor
why: Defining requirements makes her the customer and authorizing the budget makes her the sponsor; because she never uses the service, she is not a user. The other options either drop one of the roles she clearly holds or assign her the user role she does not.

q: A CFO approves funding for a help-desk contract. The operations manager specifies the response-time requirements and is held accountable when they are missed. Which statement is correct?
opts: The CFO is the sponsor and the operations manager is the customer
The CFO is the customer and the operations manager is the sponsor
Both are customers, since both are senior stakeholders in the service
The CFO is the customer and the operations manager is a user
why: Authorizing the budget is the sponsor role; defining requirements and being accountable for outcomes is the customer role. Making the CFO the customer and the manager the sponsor swaps the roles, calling both of them customers ignores that only one of them defines requirements, and calling the manager a user mislabels her when nothing says she consumes the service herself.

q: A managed service provider maps four of its value streams. Which one is a core value stream?
opts: Onboarding a newly signed client onto the managed service
Renewing the licence for the provider's internal ticketing tool
Recruiting and training new service desk analysts
Negotiating a volume discount with the provider's hardware supplier
why: Onboarding a client creates value directly for an external customer, which is what makes a value stream core. Licence renewal, recruitment, and supplier negotiation all support other value streams internally without touching the external customer, so each is an enabling value stream.

q: A software company sells a monitoring tool. For one buyer it only ships licence keys. For another it also runs the tool, watches the alerts, and agrees response targets. How should its role be classified?
opts: Digital product vendor to the first buyer, service provider to the second
Service provider to both, since both receive a product the company makes
Digital product vendor to both, since the same product is supplied each time
Service provider to the first buyer, digital product vendor to the second
why: What separates the two roles is the service relationship, not the product. Shipping keys with no ongoing provision, consumption, or relationship management makes the company a digital product vendor to the first buyer; running the tool and agreeing targets puts it in a service relationship with the second, so there it is a service provider. The other options ignore that distinction or reverse it.

q: A client reports that every target in the signed agreement was met last quarter, yet the service 'still feels poor' and users are frustrated. Which ITIL distinction best explains the gap?
opts: Service levels were met, but overall service quality fell short of expectations
The SLA was breached, because user frustration is itself a service level
Service quality was met, but the SLA was never formally agreed
There is no gap to explain, since service levels and the SLA are the same thing
why: A service level is one measured target and the SLA is the document recording those targets; service quality is how well the service meets expectations overall. Meeting every documented target while expectations go unmet is a quality gap. Frustration is not a measured service level, the agreement clearly existed, and service levels and the SLA are related but not identical.

q: A client is reviewing four commitments in a proposed identity service. Which one is a warranty commitment rather than a utility commitment?
opts: Authentication will remain available 99.9% of the time each month
Users will be able to reset their own passwords without calling the desk
New starter accounts will be created automatically from the HR system
Single sign-on will cover every application on the approved list
why: Availability is one of the four warranty aspects (availability, capacity, security, continuity) and describes how well the service performs. Self-service reset, automatic provisioning, and SSO coverage each describe what the service does, which is utility. The SSO option is the near-miss: covering every approved application sounds like a quality guarantee, but it is still scope of functionality, not a performance level.

q: A provider fixes a client's network issue free of charge after an SLA breach. Where does ITIL locate the value in this situation?
opts: In the cost the client avoided by not paying for the fix
In whatever figure the SLA document specifies for a breach
In the fix itself, whether or not the underlying issue is resolved
In the outcome the fix enables, not in the fix itself
why: Value is the perceived benefit a stakeholder realizes, which here is staff being able to work again. The fix is the mechanism, not the value. Avoided cost is only one input to the value judgement, a breach figure in the SLA is a contractual consequence rather than value, and a fix that leaves the issue unresolved has produced an output without the outcome.

q: A provider markets a service as having '99.99% availability,' but the client also needs guaranteed 4-hour incident response times to actually be satisfied. What does this illustrate?
opts: Cost is the only factor that actually determines whether customer expectations are met
Warranty covers multiple dimensions, like availability and continuity, not just an uptime number alone
Utility alone already covers response times, since both are functional capabilities of the service
Incident response time is strictly a utility concern, separate from anything warranty covers
why: Warranty spans availability, capacity, security, and continuity — a single uptime figure doesn't capture the whole picture the customer actually needs.

q: A team lead who wrote the requirements for a reporting service and also runs its reports every morning must be recorded as either the customer or the user, since one person cannot hold both roles.
opts: True
False
why: The roles are distinct in what they describe, defining requirements versus consuming the service, but nothing stops one person holding both. Recording only one would hide the fact that she is accountable for outcomes as well as affected by day-to-day usability.

q: A service that is highly available and fully secure but does not perform the function the customer actually needs can still be described as having good utility.
opts: True
False
why: Availability and security are warranty aspects, describing how well the service performs. Utility is whether it does what the customer needs, fit for purpose, so a service that misses the needed function has poor utility no matter how reliable it is.

q: A provider publishes a '99.9% uptime' target on its website, but no customer has signed an agreement referencing it. In ITIL terms this is a service level, but not yet an SLA.
opts: True
False
why: A service level is a measured target for one aspect of performance, which the published figure is. An SLA is the documented agreement between provider and customer that records such targets; until one is agreed, the target exists without an SLA behind it.

q: A value stream that never interacts with the external customer can still be classified as a core value stream provided it is business-critical.
opts: True
False
why: What makes a value stream core is that it creates value directly for the external customer, not how important it is. A business-critical internal flow, such as renewing the licences the service desk depends on, is an enabling value stream, however essential it is to keeping the core ones running.

q: A client reviews a proposed file-sync service and lists four findings. Which two relate to warranty rather than utility? (Choose two.)
opts: Files are replicated to a second region so the service continues if one region fails
Sync fails for files over 2 GB, which several engineering teams rely on
The service is sized for 5,000 concurrent users, below the 8,000 expected at peak
Folders cannot be shared with external partners
why: Continuity (regional replication) and capacity (concurrent-user sizing) are two of the four warranty aspects, describing how well the service performs. The 2 GB limit and the lack of external sharing are gaps in what the service can do, which is utility. The size limit is the near-miss because it sounds like a performance figure, but it defines functional scope rather than a performance level.

q: A support plan bundles software licenses, help desk access, and defined response times for a specific client segment. What best describes this bundle itself?
opts: A service offering
A service relationship
A value stream
A service level agreement
why: A service offering is the description of what is provided, goods, access to resources, and service actions, for a target consumer group. The ongoing cooperation once a client takes up the offering is the service relationship, a value stream is the internal sequence of steps that delivers it, and an SLA is the near-miss: it records the response-time targets but is only one documented part of the wider offering, not the bundle itself.

q: An MSP and a client sign a managed-desktop contract. Which two of the following are part of the service relationship itself, rather than something that precedes it or sits outside it? (Choose two.)
opts: The MSP delivering the agreed patching and support each month
The quarterly review where both sides adjust the device allocation
The published support-plan tiers the client chose from before signing
The laptop manufacturer's hardware warranty on the devices supplied
why: A service relationship is the ongoing cooperation made up of service provision (the monthly patching and support), service consumption, and relationship management (the quarterly review). The published tiers are the service offering, which describes what is available before any relationship exists, and the manufacturer's warranty belongs to a separate supplier arrangement outside the MSP-client relationship.

q: A team comparing two backup vendors lists four considerations. Which two are risks in ITIL's sense, rather than costs? (Choose two.)
opts: The cheaper vendor has suffered two multi-day outages this year
The premium vendor charges 40% more per terabyte stored
Choosing the cheaper vendor means forgoing an integration that would let the team retire a legacy tool
Migration will consume about 80 hours of staff time whichever vendor is chosen
why: A risk is a possible event that could cause harm or make objectives harder to reach, which covers the outage history and also the missed opportunity to retire the legacy tool, since ITIL explicitly counts lost opportunities as risk. The price premium and the migration effort are costs: resources spent on a specific activity. The missed-integration option is the one candidates most often misfile as a cost.

q: A hospital uses a scheduling application licensed from a software company and pays an MSP to configure, run, and support it. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: The MSP is the service provider to the hospital
The software company is the hospital's service provider, since it owns the product
The hospital is the service consumer, with customer, user, and sponsor roles possibly spread across different staff
The software company cannot be a digital product vendor, because its product is used inside a service relationship
why: The provider is whoever is in the service relationship delivering the service, which is the MSP; the hospital is the consumer, and its staff can hold the customer, user, and sponsor roles in any combination. Owning the product does not make the software company the provider: supplying a product without a service relationship to the hospital is exactly what a digital product vendor does, and that status is unaffected by someone else building a service on top of the product.

q: A company sells a SaaS platform (the software itself) and separately provides onboarding and support to help clients get value from it. Which is the digital product, and which is the digital service?
opts: The SaaS platform is the digital service; onboarding and support is the digital product
Both onboarding and the platform are considered digital products
The SaaS platform is the digital product; onboarding and support constitute the digital service
Both are digital services, since the client pays for them under one subscription
why: The platform itself, existing primarily in digital form, is the digital product. The value co-created through using it, including the onboarding and support that help a client get outcomes from it, is the digital service. Calling the platform the service and the onboarding the product swaps the two, calling both products collapses the difference between what is delivered and the value it enables, and how the client is billed does not change which part is the product.

q: A software company that only licenses a product to an organization, with no provision, consumption, or relationship-management activities between them, is still that organization's service provider because it owns the product.
opts: True
False
why: Owning the product does not create a service relationship. With none of the relationship activities present, the company is a digital product vendor; the service provider is whoever is actually in the service relationship with the organization, which may be an MSP running the product on its behalf, or the organization's own IT team.

q: In a managed-service contract, the client's CFO funds it, its IT director sets the requirements, and its 400 staff raise the tickets. The MSP's account manager keeps referring to 'the consumer'. Who is she referring to?
opts: The client organization as a whole, across all three roles
Only the 400 staff, since they consume the service day to day
Only the IT director, since the consumer is whoever defines requirements
The MSP itself, since it consumes the client's budget
why: The consumer is the party receiving the service, and that party can hold the sponsor, customer, and user roles across different people. Narrowing it to the staff confuses consumer with user, narrowing it to the director confuses consumer with customer, and the MSP is the provider, not the consumer.

q: A team chooses a cheaper hosting provider with a weaker outage track record, planning to accept the occasional downtime instead of paying for a premium, more reliable option. What trade-off does this decision represent?
opts: Lower cost accepted in exchange for higher risk
Lower risk accepted in exchange for higher cost
Lower utility accepted in exchange for higher warranty
Lower warranty accepted in exchange for higher utility
why: Cost and risk trade off against each other -- spending less here means accepting a greater chance of a costly outage. Utility and warranty describe the service's own functional and reliability qualities, not a financial choice between hosting providers, so framing this specific trade-off in those terms swaps in the wrong pair of concepts.

q: A managed print contract lists two printer models, a monthly ticket allowance, and a 4-hour response time. Six months in, the account manager is also running renewal conversations and adjusting the ticket allowance to actual usage. Which term captures that ongoing account work specifically, as opposed to what the contract lists?
opts: The service relationship
The service offering
A management practice
The digital product vendor role
why: The contract's fixed list of printers, tickets, and response times is the service offering. The renewal conversations and usage-based adjustments are relationship management activities, which together with provision and consumption make up the service relationship. 'Account management' is not one of ITIL's 34 named practices, and supplying hardware does not make this a vendor-only arrangement when ongoing support commitments are part of the deal.

q: A provider adds a costly redundant failover system, and customers still consider the service worth paying for afterward because outages are now rare. What term describes that overall perceived worth, weighing the added cost against the reduced risk?
opts: Warranty
Value
Output
Outcome
why: Value is the perceived worth a stakeholder assigns once utility and warranty are weighed against cost and risk, which is the judgement the customers are making. Warranty is only the improved availability itself, the failover system is an output, and rare outages are the outcome; the question asks about the overall weighing of that outcome against the added cost.

q: Buying an ITSM tool suite with incident, request, and change modules gives an organization service management capability, since the tool supplies the processes.
opts: True
False
why: Service management is a set of organizational capabilities spanning people, process, information, and technology working together. A tool is one technology input; without skilled people, agreed processes, and reliable information the capability does not exist, which is why tool purchases alone so often fail to improve service.

q: A team documents clear, structured steps for logging and routing a ticket, but has no defined people, tools, or other resources organized around those steps yet. What's missing to call this a full management practice rather than just a process?
opts: Nothing; a process and a practice are the same thing
The people, tools, and other resources organized around the steps
A governance decision authorizing the steps
A value stream for the steps to belong to
why: A practice is the broader bundle: people, tools, information, and other resources organized around one or more processes to accomplish an objective; a process alone is just the structured set of activities. Governance authorization is not what turns a process into a practice, and a value stream is a separate construct that would use the practice rather than complete it.

q: A hospital's patient-portal service is under review. Which two of the following are stakeholders in the service even though none of them is its customer, user, or sponsor? (Choose two.)
opts: The health regulator that audits how patient data is handled
The hospital's internal auditor assessing the portal's access controls
The nurse who logs in each shift to update patient records
The operations director who signed off the portal's budget
why: A stakeholder is anyone with an interest in or expectations of an activity or decision, so the regulator and the internal auditor qualify without using, funding, or specifying the service. The nurse is a user and the operations director is the sponsor: both are stakeholders too, but they hold one of the three named roles, which the question excludes.

q: A shareholder who has never used the company's online-banking service, and is neither its customer nor its sponsor, cannot be a stakeholder in that service.
opts: True
False
why: Stakeholder requires only an interest in or expectations of an activity or decision. A shareholder has a clear interest in whether the service protects revenue and reputation, so they qualify without holding any of the customer, user, or sponsor roles, just as a regulator or auditor would.

q: A consultant's slide lists the five components of the ITIL Value System as guiding principles, governance, the value chain, the four dimensions, and continual improvement. Which correction is needed?
opts: Replace the four dimensions with management practices
Replace governance with the service desk
Replace the value chain with value streams
Replace continual improvement with the Continual Improvement Model
why: The five components are guiding principles, governance, the value chain, management practices, and continual improvement. The four dimensions are a separate model that sits alongside the Value System, not inside it. The service desk is a practice, value streams are built from the value chain rather than replacing it, and the Continual Improvement Model is the method used by the continual improvement component, not a substitute for it.

q: A team inherits a twelve-step ticketing workflow. One manager wants to scrap it and design a replacement from a blank page. Another wants to measure how the current workflow actually performs before deciding what to change. Which principle does the second approach reflect most directly?
opts: Start where you are
Keep it simple and practical
Progress iteratively with feedback
Focus on value
why: Start where you are means assessing the current state honestly and reusing what works instead of rebuilding by default. Keep it simple and practical is the near-miss: it may well apply once the measurement shows which steps add nothing, but the decision described is about assessing first. Progress iteratively concerns how change is delivered in steps, and focus on value concerns tracing work to stakeholder benefit.

q: A team spends four hours each week compiling a status report. When asked, nobody can name who reads it or what decision it informs. Which principle most directly says the report itself should be questioned?
opts: Focus on value
Keep it simple and practical
Optimize and automate
Start where you are
why: Focus on value asks whether an activity maps to any stakeholder outcome at all; if nobody benefits, the work should be challenged rather than refined. Keep it simple and practical would trim steps out of a report that is still worth producing, and optimize and automate would make it quicker to produce, but both assume the report should exist. Start where you are is about assessing the current state before changing it.

q: A poster of the guiding principles reads: focus on value; start where you are; progress iteratively with feedback; collaborate and promote visibility; think and work holistically; keep it simple and practical; standardize before improving. What is wrong with it?
opts: 'Standardize before improving' should be 'optimize and automate'
'Start where you are' is not a guiding principle and should be removed
'Continual improvement' is missing and should be added as an eighth principle
Nothing; the poster lists all seven principles correctly
why: There are seven principles and the seventh is optimize and automate; 'standardize before improving' sounds plausible but is not one of them. Start where you are is genuine, and continual improvement is a separate Value System component rather than a principle, so adding it would be a second error.

q: A company's board sets a policy that no supplier may be onboarded without a security assessment, reviews each quarter whether the policy is being followed, and tightens it after an audit finding. Which Value System component is the board exercising?
opts: Governance
A management practice
Continual improvement
The guiding principles
why: Directing (setting the policy), monitoring (quarterly review), and evaluating (adjusting after the audit) are the three governance activities. The supplier management practice is what carries the policy out day to day. Continual improvement is the near-miss because the policy was tightened, but the board is acting in its direct-and-control role, not running an improvement initiative. The guiding principles are recommendations, not a mechanism for mandating and policing a rule.

q: A change process has three approval steps. Two repeat a check an automated scanner already performs; the third is a genuine risk review. The team deletes the two duplicates, keeps the third exactly as it is, and automates nothing. Which principle have they applied?
opts: Keep it simple and practical
Optimize and automate
Start where you are
Focus on value
why: Removing steps that contribute nothing while keeping the one that does is keep it simple and practical. Optimize and automate is the near-miss, but nothing here was automated and the act described is purely step reduction. Start where you are would describe assessing the existing process before touching it, and focus on value is the broader test of whether work maps to an outcome at all.

q: A manager builds a monthly review into every team's routine: each team checks whether its service still meets stakeholder expectations and proposes small adjustments, whether or not any project is running. Which Value System component is being put into practice?
opts: Continual improvement
Governance
The value chain
Management practices
why: A recurring activity, performed across every part of the organization, to keep performance aligned with stakeholder expectations is the definition of continual improvement. Governance is the near-miss because it also involves reviewing performance, but governance is leadership-level direction and control, not every team adjusting its own work. The value chain is the operating model that converts demand into value, and management practices are the resources used to do the work.

q: A team pilots a new ticketing system with one department, then rolls it out company-wide on the planned date without reviewing anything the pilot department reported. Which principle was only partly applied?
opts: Progress iteratively with feedback
Start where you are
Collaborate and promote visibility
Think and work holistically
why: The team did progress iteratively, but the principle requires each iteration to be checked against real feedback before the next step; skipping the pilot review is the half that was missed. Start where you are concerns assessing the current state before change, collaborate and promote visibility concerns openness about work in progress, and think and work holistically concerns ripple effects across the organization.

q: Two support teams each run a separate incident queue and neither can see the other's open tickets. Both spend a day investigating the same outage before anyone notices the duplication. Which principle, applied earlier, would most directly have prevented this?
opts: Collaborate and promote visibility
Think and work holistically
Keep it simple and practical
Optimize and automate
why: The failure is hidden work: nobody could see what the other team was doing. Making work and progress visible across boundaries is collaborate and promote visibility. Think and work holistically is the near-miss, but it concerns understanding how a change in one area affects another, not whether work is visible. Keep it simple and optimize and automate address process waste and manual effort, not the lack of shared information.

q: An organization's incident management capability consists of trained analysts, a ticketing tool, documented procedures, and a knowledge base, all organized to restore service when something breaks. In Value System terms, this bundle is best described as:
opts: A management practice
A value stream
A value chain activity
A governance control
why: A set of organizational resources, people, tools, processes, and information, assembled to perform a kind of work is a management practice. A value stream would be an end-to-end sequence for one scenario, such as resolving a specific incident from report to closure. Support is the value chain activity the practice contributes to, not the bundle of resources itself, and a governance control is a directive from leadership rather than a working capability.

q: A manager insists on adding a new approval step 'because that's how we've always handled security,' even though it duplicates a check already performed elsewhere. Which principle is most directly being violated?
opts: Focus on value
Keep it simple and practical
Collaborate and promote visibility
Start where you are
why: A redundant step that duplicates an existing check works against using the minimum number of steps needed — the core idea of keep it simple and practical.

q: A manual approval step is slow, error-prone, and also redundant with an earlier check. In what order should the guiding principles be applied here?
opts: Apply both simultaneously with no particular order, since sequencing guiding principles doesn't matter
Optimize and automate first, then simplify afterward, since automation naturally reveals which steps are redundant
Neither principle applies here, since automation decisions fall under governance instead of the guiding principles
Keep it simple and practical first, removing the redundant step, then optimize and automate what remains
why: Automating a broken process just makes it fail faster — simplify first, then automate what's left.

q: A manager describes the service desk, incident management, and change enablement as three of the five components of the ITIL Value System.
opts: True
False
why: All three are individual management practices. Management practices as a whole form one of the five components, alongside the guiding principles, governance, the value chain, and continual improvement; naming three practices as separate components confuses the contents of one component with the list itself.

q: Because governance guides decisions in every circumstance, ITIL lists it among the seven guiding principles.
opts: True
False
why: Governance is a separate Value System component: the means by which the organization is directed and controlled through evaluating, directing, and monitoring. The guiding principles are recommendations for how to act; governance is the mechanism that sets and enforces policy, which is why the two are kept apart.

q: A team automates its existing five-step approval flow exactly as it stands, planning to remove any redundant steps once the automation is running. This matches the sequence that optimize and automate recommends.
opts: True
False
why: The principle is optimize first, then automate what remains. Automating the flow as-is bakes the redundant steps into the new tooling, so removing them afterwards means reworking the automation; the waste should have been stripped out before anything was automated.

q: Once a continual improvement initiative has hit its target, the Continual Improvement Model is complete for that service and the organization moves on to the next priority.
opts: True
False
why: The model's final step, how do we keep the momentum going, exists precisely because hitting a target is not the end: continual improvement is a recurring activity across the whole organization, so gains have to be sustained and the cycle revisited rather than closed out.

q: A desk analyst deciding how to phrase a single status update to a frustrated user is a situation the guiding principles are intended to apply to.
opts: True
False
why: The principles are deliberately generic so they guide behaviour in every circumstance, from a one-line ticket update (focus on value, collaborate and promote visibility) to a whole restructuring. Reserving them for large formal initiatives is the misreading the exam likes to test.

q: A team cites 'start where you are' to justify keeping a legacy tool, even though their own measurements show it causes most of their delays. This is a correct application of the principle.
opts: True
False
why: Start where you are means measuring the current state honestly and reusing what genuinely works; it is a starting point for informed change, not a reason to avoid it. When the measurements show the tool is the main source of delay, the principle supports replacing it, not defending it.

q: A team sets a measurable, time-bound target for cutting incident resolution time in half before building an action plan to get there. Which step of the Continual Improvement Model are they in?
opts: Where do we want to be?
What is the vision?
How do we get there?
Did we get there?
why: Setting a measurable, time-bound target is exactly the 'where do we want to be' step. It comes after assessing the current state and before building the action plan in 'how do we get there.'

q: A team builds a detailed action plan to improve response times but never measured how long responses currently take. Which step of the Continual Improvement Model did they skip?
opts: Where are we now?
What is the vision?
Take action
How do we keep the momentum going?
why: Without an honest baseline from 'where are we now,' any target or plan built afterward is just a guess. The steps depend on the ones before them.

q: After migrating to a new ticketing system, a team discovers that reports another department relies on, pulled from the old system, are now broken. Which guiding principle would have surfaced this risk earlier?
opts: Think and work holistically
Keep it simple and practical
Focus on value
Start where you are
why: Think and work holistically means recognizing how a change ripples across the wider organization rather than just the team making it. Missing a downstream dependency like this is exactly what the principle is meant to prevent.

q: Two trainers disagree. One teaches the value chain as an older six-activity model, with the eight-stage lifecycle as a separate thing to memorize. The other teaches that the value chain component is expressed as the eight-stage lifecycle. Under the current model, who is right?
opts: The second trainer: the eight-stage lifecycle is how the value chain component is expressed
The first trainer: the six activities remain the value chain, and the lifecycle is an operational view
Both: an organization may adopt either model as its value chain
Neither: the value chain was dropped and the four dimensions took its place
why: The value chain is still a Value System component, an operating model converting demand into value, and it is expressed as Discover, Design, Acquire, Build, Transition, Operate, Deliver, Support. There is no second six-activity list to learn alongside it, it is not optional, and the four dimensions are a separate model rather than a replacement.

q: The Continual Improvement Model's steps can be completed in any order, since improvement work isn't linear.
opts: True
False
why: The steps build on each other in sequence, from vision through momentum. You can loop back to an earlier step as understanding improves, but you can't meaningfully skip ahead, like setting a target before knowing where you're starting from.

q: A team drafts four 'working agreements'. Which two restate an ITIL guiding principle, rather than something ITIL does not actually recommend? (Choose two.)
opts: Ship small changes and review how each one landed before starting the next
Remove manual effort only after the process it supports has been streamlined
Standardize every team on one process before any improvement work begins
Build each new service from a clean slate to avoid inheriting legacy problems
why: The first is progress iteratively with feedback and the second is optimize and automate in its correct order. Standardizing before improving is not a principle and conflicts with keep it simple and practical, and starting from a clean slate is the opposite of start where you are, which asks teams to assess and reuse what already exists.

q: Which two of the following situations are failures of think and work holistically, rather than of collaborate and promote visibility? (Choose two.)
opts: A network change passes testing but silently breaks a finance report that relied on the old route
An SLA is agreed for one service without noticing it depends on a supplier whose own targets are looser
Two teams investigate the same outage because neither can see the other's queue
A project's risk register is kept in a private spreadsheet until the monthly steering meeting
why: The first two are missed dependencies: a change or a commitment made without seeing how it connects to the rest of the system, which is what think and work holistically guards against. The other two are hidden work and hidden information, which is the domain of collaborate and promote visibility. Both principles concern openness, but one is about understanding connections and the other about sharing what is happening.

q: Which two statements correctly describe how ITIL's management practices are organized and used? (Choose two.)
opts: The 34 practices divide into general management practices and product and service management practices
A single practice can contribute to many different value streams
Each practice maps to exactly one lifecycle activity
Technical management practices form a third, separate group in the current model
why: The current model groups the 34 practices into 12 general management and 22 product and service management practices, and any practice, incident management for instance, can be drawn into whichever value streams need it. Practices are not tied to a single lifecycle activity, and the separate technical management group from older material no longer exists.

q: A team's improvement write-up contains four statements. Which two correspond to a step of the Continual Improvement Model? (Choose two.)
opts: 'Average resolution time is currently 9.5 hours, measured over the last quarter'
'We will track the new figure monthly and revisit the target in six months'
'The vendor has agreed a 10% discount on the new tooling'
'The change advisory board met twice this month'
why: The measured baseline is 'where are we now?' and the plan to keep tracking and revisiting is 'how do we keep the momentum going?'. A vendor discount and a board meeting are ordinary project events; neither is a step of the model, whose seven steps run from 'what is the vision?' through to sustaining momentum.

q: A consultant maps parts of an organization onto the ITIL Value System. Which two mappings are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: The board's policy that every change needs a documented risk assessment: governance
The incident management team with its tooling and procedures: management practices
The 'resolve an incident' flow from first report to closure: the value chain
The four-dimensions checklist used in design reviews: continual improvement
why: A leadership mandate is governance, and a team with its tools and procedures organized for one kind of work is a management practice. The incident flow is a value stream built from value chain activities, not the value chain itself, which is the near-miss. The four dimensions are a separate model and are not a Value System component at all.

q: A new service manager asks what the value chain component actually is, given that her team already has practices and value streams. Which answer is correct?
opts: The master list of all 34 practices and which team owns each one
The single value stream that handles the organization's most important service
The set of policies through which leadership directs the practices
The operating model of activities that value streams draw on to turn demand into value
why: The value chain is an operating model, expressed as the eight lifecycle activities, from which every value stream selects the activities a scenario needs. The practice list is the management practices component, a single flow is one value stream rather than the chain they all draw on, and policies from leadership are governance.

q: A support team holds a daily 10-minute standup where they openly share which incidents are open, blocked, or at risk, so other departments can see the current state without having to ask. Which guiding principle is this most directly an example of?
opts: Collaborate and promote visibility
Think and work holistically
Progress iteratively with feedback
Optimize and automate
why: Openly sharing current status so others can see what's happening without asking is exactly collaborate and promote visibility. It isn't specifically about ripple effects across the organization (think and work holistically), incremental delivery (progress iteratively with feedback), or reducing manual effort (optimize and automate).

q: Leadership sets a policy requiring every improvement initiative to report progress against a documented baseline before it can move on to planning how it will get there. Which two Value System concepts does this combine?
opts: Governance and the Continual Improvement Model
Two guiding principles applied together
The value chain and a value stream
Management practices and the four dimensions
why: Leadership mandating a rule is governance directing and controlling how work happens, and the baseline-before-plan sequence it enforces is the Continual Improvement Model's 'where are we now?' and 'how do we get there?' steps. No guiding principle mandates anything, the value chain and value streams describe how work flows rather than policy, and the four dimensions are not a Value System component.

q: A team wants to reduce the seven manual fields analysts fill out when closing a ticket. Three of those fields duplicate data already captured elsewhere in the ticketing system. Their first move is to build a bot that auto-fills all seven fields exactly as analysts currently type them, including the three duplicates. What did the team get wrong?
opts: They automated before simplifying, so the redundant fields are now built into the bot
Nothing; automating first reveals which fields can be simplified later
They applied the wrong principle; field counts are governed by focus on value, not optimize and automate
They breached start where you are by changing the analysts' manual process at all
why: Optimize and automate calls for simplifying first and automating what remains; automating with the three duplicate fields still in place makes the redundancy run faster and harder to remove. Automating first and simplifying later has the order reversed, focus on value does not govern step reduction the way keep it simple and practical does, and start where you are means assessing what exists, not refusing to change it.

q: A migration project is broken into quarterly releases, with each one adjusted based on what users report after the previous release goes live. Which guiding principle does this best demonstrate?
opts: Think and work holistically
Progress iteratively with feedback
Optimize and automate
Start where you are
why: Breaking work into smaller pieces, checking it against real feedback, and adjusting before the next piece is exactly progress iteratively with feedback.

q: Before a database upgrade, a project manager publishes the change plan on a shared board, invites support, finance, and security to comment, and posts daily progress so anyone can see where it stands. Which guiding principle is most directly illustrated?
opts: Collaborate and promote visibility
Think and work holistically
Progress iteratively with feedback
Keep it simple and practical
why: Opening the plan to other teams, inviting their input, and making progress visible is collaborate and promote visibility. Think and work holistically is the near-miss: it would be the better fit if the scenario emphasized analysing how the upgrade affects downstream systems, but what is described is openness and involvement. No incremental delivery or step reduction is mentioned.

q: Think and work holistically is satisfied when a team makes its change plan visible to other teams, even if nobody checks how the change will affect their systems.
opts: True
False
why: Making the plan visible is collaborate and promote visibility. Think and work holistically requires actually understanding how the change connects to and affects other parts of the organization; publishing a plan nobody analyses for impact leaves exactly the downstream breakage the principle exists to prevent.

q: A service desk wants to automate ticket categorization. Which two actions are consistent with the guiding principle optimize and automate? (Choose two.)
opts: First merging the 40 overlapping categories into the 12 analysts actually use
Measuring how often current categories get corrected later, before deciding what to automate
Automating all 40 existing categories as they are, so the model can learn which are redundant
Leaving categorization manual, since the principle applies only when a whole process is replaced
why: The principle is to understand and streamline a process first, then automate what remains, so consolidating the categories and measuring the current error rate both come before any automation. Automating the 40 categories as-is bakes the redundancy into the model, and the principle applies to any work where human effort can be reduced, not only wholesale replacement of a manual process.

q: Leadership mandates that every production change must include a documented rollback plan. The team that actually writes and tests each specific rollback plan is performing:
opts: Governance
A management practice
A guiding principle
Continual improvement
why: Leadership's mandate is governance, directing and controlling from the top; the team that writes and tests each rollback plan is carrying the mandate out with organizational resources, which is a management practice (change enablement). Governance is the near-miss because the rule came from leadership, but the question asks about the team doing the work. No guiding principle produces a plan, and continual improvement would describe reviewing and refining the rule over time.

q: A change manager who assesses, authorizes, and schedules each normal change is performing governance, because authorizing changes is a form of control.
opts: True
False
why: Governance is the governing body evaluating, directing, and monitoring the organization as a whole, for example mandating that every change be risk-assessed. Assessing and authorizing individual changes under that mandate is the change enablement practice at work: a management practice carrying out the direction, not the direction itself.

q: A company adopts a remote-first policy. Support analysts now need coaching on diagnosing problems over video calls, and the escalation path is redrawn around who is online rather than who sits nearest. Which dimensions do the coaching and the redrawn escalation path belong to, respectively?
opts: Organizations and people; value streams and processes
Value streams and processes; organizations and people
Organizations and people; information and technology
Information and technology; value streams and processes
why: New skills for staff sit under organizations and people, and how an escalation flows from one step to the next is a workflow matter under value streams and processes. Listing them the other way round reverses them. Information and technology would cover the video tooling itself, which the scenario does not describe as changing.

q: A new data-privacy law forces a company to move where customer records are stored, retrain staff on handling access requests, and renegotiate its hosting contract. How should the law itself be classified?
opts: An external PESTLE factor influencing several dimensions at once
Part of the information and technology dimension, since it concerns data
Part of the partners and suppliers dimension, since a contract must change
A fifth dimension that sits alongside the other four
why: The law is a Legal factor in the external environment; its effects land in information and technology, organizations and people, and partners and suppliers, but the law itself belongs to none of them. The two dimension options each name only one consequence and mistake it for the cause, and PESTLE factors are pressures on the four dimensions rather than a dimension of their own.

q: A hospital's records platform is hosted by a third party. After a slow-performance complaint, the IT lead finds the platform's own configuration is sound, but the hosting contract contains no capacity-review clause. Which dimension does the gap she identified sit in?
opts: Partners and suppliers
Information and technology
Value streams and processes
Organizations and people
why: The weakness is in the terms of a relationship with an external organization, which is the partners and suppliers dimension. Information and technology is the near-miss because the symptom is technical, but the scenario says the technology itself is sound. No workflow or staffing gap is described.

q: Which of the following is an example of a PESTLE factor, rather than a change inside one of the four dimensions?
opts: A national election brings in a government promising new procurement rules
A supplier announces it will end support for a product the company depends on
A reorganization merges two internal support teams into one
The company moves its ticketing tool onto a new platform
why: A change of government is a Political factor in the wider environment that the organization cannot control. The supplier announcement is a near-miss because it is external, but it is a specific relationship within the partners and suppliers dimension, not a macro-environmental pressure. The merger sits in organizations and people and the platform move in information and technology.

q: A company replaces its manual password-reset procedure with an automation built by its own developers, freeing analysts for other work. No external vendor is involved. Which dimension is least directly affected by this change?
opts: Partners and suppliers
Information and technology
Organizations and people
Value streams and processes
why: The automation is new technology, the retired manual procedure is a workflow change, and the shift in analyst workload touches people and roles, so three dimensions move. Because the work was done in-house with no vendor, partners and suppliers is the one dimension the scenario leaves essentially untouched.

q: A company outsources network monitoring to a third party, who then requires in-house staff to be trained to interpret their alerts correctly. Which two dimensions are directly involved?
opts: Partners and suppliers, and organizations and people
Partners and suppliers, and information and technology
Information and technology, and organizations and people
Value streams and processes, and partners and suppliers
why: The outsourcing relationship sits under partners and suppliers, and the training need sits under organizations and people. Information and technology is the tempting near-miss because monitoring is technical, but the scenario describes no change to the tooling itself, and no workflow redesign is mentioned either.

q: Because a new regulation dictates how a company must store customer data, the regulation itself becomes part of the information and technology dimension.
opts: True
False
why: The regulation is a Legal factor in the external PESTLE environment. Its consequences land inside the dimensions, here in information and technology, and probably in organizations and people and partners and suppliers too, but the external pressure stays outside all four; confusing the cause with where its effects land is the error.

q: A change that appears confined to the information and technology dimension, such as swapping one monitoring tool for another, can generally be planned without reviewing the other three dimensions.
opts: True
False
why: The dimensions interact: a new monitoring tool typically changes who needs which skills (organizations and people), may introduce a new vendor (partners and suppliers), and alters how alerts flow (value streams and processes). Treating a change as single-dimension is how the ripple effects get missed.

q: A single software licence bought from a vendor with no support contract attached still falls within the partners and suppliers dimension.
opts: True
False
why: The dimension covers every relationship with another organization involved in providing the service, from a one-off licence purchase to a full outsourcing arrangement. Scale and formality do not decide whether something belongs here; the involvement of an external organization does.

q: A company's rollout of an AI ticket-triage assistant requires staff to learn how to review and override its recommendations. Beyond information and technology, which dimension is most directly affected?
opts: Organizations and people
Partners and suppliers
Value streams and processes
None; it is a technology change only
why: New skills, oversight responsibilities, and changed roles for staff sit under organizations and people, and the current model explicitly recognizes AI adoption as touching this dimension. Value streams and processes is the near-miss, since the triage workflow also shifts, but the scenario describes what staff must learn to do, not a redrawn process. No external supplier is mentioned, and treating it as technology-only is the mistake the dimensions exist to prevent.

q: A post-incident review lists four contributing causes. Which two belong to the organizations and people dimension? (Choose two.)
opts: The on-call engineer had never been trained on the new storage platform
Nobody was clearly accountable for approving the vendor's emergency patch
The monitoring tool's alert threshold had been set too high to fire
The hosting contract gave the vendor 24 hours to respond to critical issues
why: Skills and clear accountability are both organizations and people matters. The alert threshold is a configuration issue in information and technology, and the contractual response time sits in partners and suppliers. The accountability gap is the near-miss because a vendor is involved, but the missing piece is an internal role, not the contract.

q: A government passes a data-residency law; a currency slump makes overseas hosting 30% more expensive; and public pressure is growing over how companies use customer data. Which option labels these three PESTLE factors in order?
opts: Legal, Economic, Social
Political, Economic, Social
Legal, Technological, Political
Political, Legal, Social
why: An enacted law creating a compliance requirement is Legal, a currency movement is Economic, and shifting public attitudes are Social. Political is the near-miss for the first item, but Political covers government stability and policy direction, whereas a law already in force is Legal. Nothing in the scenario describes a technology trend.

q: After an AI triage assistant is introduced, deciding who may override its recommendations and who is accountable when it is wrong belongs to the organizations and people dimension.
opts: True
False
why: Roles, responsibilities, and accountability are organizations and people matters, and the current model explicitly extends that dimension to the skills and oversight duties AI creates. The assistant itself sits in information and technology, which is why candidates often misfile the accountability question there too.

q: After acquiring a smaller IT provider, a company must integrate the acquired firm's outsourced backup-monitoring vendor into its own workflows, redesigning how a backup-failure alert gets routed and escalated. Which two dimensions does this integration touch most directly?
opts: Partners and suppliers, and value streams and processes
Partners and suppliers, and information and technology
Organizations and people, and value streams and processes
Information and technology, and organizations and people
why: The outsourced vendor relationship sits under partners and suppliers, and redesigning how an alert is routed and escalated is a workflow change under value streams and processes. Information and technology is the tempting near-miss because backups are technical, but the scenario describes no tooling change, and no retraining or role change is mentioned for organizations and people.

q: A routine password reset request passes through four separate approval systems before completion, even though staffing, tools, and vendor relationships are all fine. Which dimension does this problem sit in?
opts: Organizations and people
Value streams and processes
Partners and suppliers
Information and technology
why: Unnecessary steps and handoffs in how a request actually moves are a value streams and processes problem, not a staffing, tooling, or vendor issue.

q: A company moves its hardware-support contract to a new supplier whose engineers now attend site, and makes one of its own analysts the supplier's named point of contact with a new set of responsibilities. The tooling and the request workflow are unchanged. Which two dimensions does this touch most directly? (Choose two.)
opts: Partners and suppliers
Organizations and people
Information and technology
Value streams and processes
why: A new supplier relationship sits under partners and suppliers, and a changed role with new responsibilities for an in-house analyst sits under organizations and people. The scenario explicitly rules out a tooling change (information and technology) and a workflow change (value streams and processes), which is what makes the other two options distractors rather than extra answers.

q: A team has defined the requirements for a new service and bought its core component from a supplier. Its developers now need to write the integration code that connects that component to existing systems. Which activity are they entering, and which did they just complete?
opts: Entering Build, having completed Acquire
Entering Transition, having completed Build
Entering Acquire, having completed Design
Entering Build, having completed Design
why: The lifecycle runs Discover, Design, Acquire, Build, Transition, Operate, Deliver, Support. Buying the component was Acquire, and writing integration code is Build. Entering Build having completed Design is the near-miss: Design was completed earlier, but the purchase that followed it is the activity just finished. Transition only begins once there is something assembled to test and release.

q: Before anyone writes a requirement for a self-service reset tool, a team interviews branch staff about how often they get locked out and what they do while waiting for the desk. Which lifecycle activity is this?
opts: Discover
Design
Acquire
Operate
why: Understanding demand and whether a real problem exists, before anything is specified, is Discover. Design is the near-miss because the findings will feed requirements, but the scenario stresses that no requirement has been written yet. Acquire obtains components and Operate runs a live service.

q: A new payroll service has passed user-acceptance testing and is being released to all staff during a weekend cut-over, with a rollback plan on standby. Which lifecycle activity is this?
opts: Transition
Deliver
Build
Operate
why: Moving a new or changed service into live use, including testing and release, is Transition. Deliver is the near-miss, but it describes providing agreed outcomes to consumers once the service is live, not the cut-over itself. Build assembles the solution before testing, and Operate is the day-to-day running that starts after the release.

q: Three months after go-live: (1) the platform team applies routine patches and watches capacity; (2) the desk restores access for a user who was locked out; (3) staff submit expense claims through the tool. Which option maps (1), (2), and (3) to lifecycle activities?
opts: Operate, Support, Deliver
Support, Operate, Deliver
Operate, Deliver, Support
Deliver, Support, Operate
why: Running the service day to day is Operate, fixing an issue a user hits is Support, and staff obtaining the agreed outcome is Deliver. The other options swap at least one pair; the most common slip is labelling routine running as Support, which is reserved for resolving issues and requests.

q: A team is introducing a third-party identity component. Which of the following actions belongs to the Acquire activity rather than Design, Build, or Transition?
opts: Signing the licence agreement for the identity component
Writing the security specification the component must satisfy
Coding the connector that links the component to the HR system
Running the pilot with one department before wider release
why: Acquire means obtaining components from suppliers, which the licence agreement is. The specification is Design, the connector is in-house development under Build, and the pilot is part of Transition. All four are steps in the same project, so the question turns on which activity each one belongs to rather than on recognizing the project.

q: A team already has an approved design and is now assembling a solution using one in-house component and one purchased component. Which two activities are they most likely in?
opts: Transition and Operate
Deliver and Support
Discover and Design
Build and Acquire
why: Acquire covers the purchased component, Build covers the in-house one — both come after Design.

q: The eight lifecycle activities are generally performed in a single pass from Discover through Support, with looping back to an earlier activity treated as a sign the process broke down.
opts: True
False
why: They're used iteratively by design — looping back to an earlier activity, like returning to Design after issues surface in Build, is expected and normal, not a sign of failure.

q: A platform team's routine patching, capacity monitoring, and nightly batch runs belong to the Support activity of the lifecycle, since they keep users supported.
opts: True
False
why: Routine day-to-day running of a live service is Operate. Support is reserved for responding to the issues and requests users raise while using the service, so keeping the platform healthy in the background and fixing a user's broken access are two different activities, even though both happen after go-live.

q: Because Acquire and Build both produce components for the same product, a project is expected to use one or the other rather than both.
opts: True
False
why: Acquire obtains components from suppliers and Build develops them in house, and a single project routinely does both, for example buying an identity-verification component while coding the workflow around it. The two activities are complementary routes to a deployable result, not alternatives.

q: A project plan lists four work packages. Which two sit in the Transition activity of the Product and Service Lifecycle? (Choose two.)
opts: Running user-acceptance testing against the assembled solution
Releasing the solution to the first wave of branch offices
Writing the interface specification the supplier must meet
Handling the first month of user-reported defects after go-live
why: Transition covers moving a new or changed service into live use, which includes testing and release. The interface specification is Design work, and dealing with defects reported by users once live is Support. The defects option is the near-miss: it follows release closely, but by then the service is in use and the activity has moved on.

q: A payroll service is live. Which of the following is an example of the Deliver activity, as distinct from Operate, Support, or Transition?
opts: The platform team running the overnight payroll batch and monitoring it
Employees receiving correct payslips on the agreed date each month
The desk correcting a payslip an employee reports as wrong
The release team cutting over to the new payroll version
why: Deliver is the consumer actually receiving the agreed outcome, which is the payslip arriving correctly and on time. Running and monitoring the batch is Operate, fixing a reported error is Support, and the version cut-over is Transition. The batch run is the near-miss because it produces the payslips, but it is the internal running of the service rather than the outcome reaching the consumer.

q: A team that has completed the Design activity has, by definition, already placed the orders for the components the design calls for.
opts: True
False
why: Design produces requirements and specifications; obtaining components from suppliers is Acquire, the activity that follows. The boundary matters because a specification can still change cheaply, whereas a placed order commits money and supplier time.

q: A team has already piloted a new expense-reporting tool with one department and is now making it available to all employees, after which the platform team will keep it running day to day. Which two lifecycle activities are happening here, in order?
opts: Transition, then Operate
Transition, then Support
Design, then Build
Discover, then Deliver
why: Moving from a limited pilot into full live availability is Transition, and running the tool day to day afterward is Operate. Support would instead mean resolving issues and requests rather than routine day-to-day running, and Design/Build or Discover/Deliver describe earlier or different activities than what's happening in this scenario.

q: A team is in the Build activity when testing reveals the original requirements were incomplete. What should happen next, given how the Product and Service Lifecycle is meant to work?
opts: Keep building and fix the requirements later during Support
Loop back to Design to address the gap before continuing
Restart the lifecycle from Discover, since the model runs one way
Move on to Transition and record the gap as a known error
why: The lifecycle is iterative by design, so returning to Design when Build exposes a requirements gap is the expected move, not a failure. Deferring the fix to Support ships a known gap to users, restarting from Discover throws away valid work and misreads the model as linear, and a known error is a problem-management record for a live fault, not a way to carry an unresolved requirement into release.

q: A manager already has a list of the four practices involved in fulfilling access requests, yet still cannot explain why requests take five days when the hands-on work totals forty minutes. What would value stream mapping add?
opts: Where in the end-to-end sequence requests sit waiting rather than progressing
The service level targets each of the four practices is committed to
The share of the fulfilment budget each practice consumes
How mature each of the four practices is relative to the others
why: Value stream mapping lays out every step in order with the time spent working versus waiting, which is exactly what a list of practices cannot show. Service level targets come from service level management, budget allocation is a financial exercise, and a maturity ranking assesses practices individually rather than how work flows between them.

q: A service desk lead designs an 'onboard a new employee' flow that draws on lifecycle activities from Discover through Support and assigns the request, access, and asset practices to specific steps. What has she produced?
opts: A value stream
A new value chain
A management practice
A service offering
why: Combining value chain activities and practices into an end-to-end sequence for one specific scenario is a value stream. She has not created a new value chain, which is the single operating model all value streams draw from, nor a practice, which is one set of resources for one kind of work. A service offering describes what is provided to a consumer group, not how the work flows internally.

q: A team wants to see whether a request typically waits longest at the approval step or the fulfillment step. Which technique would they use?
opts: Service level management
The Continual Improvement Model
Value stream mapping
PESTLE analysis
why: Value stream mapping visualizes each step of a value stream with the time spent waiting versus working, so it shows exactly where delay accumulates. Service level management tracks whether targets are met but not where time goes inside the flow, the Continual Improvement Model is the overall improvement framework within which mapping might be used, and PESTLE analysis looks at external environmental factors.

q: Value stream mapping is most useful once, at the start of a redesign; repeating it after the changes go live adds little, because the steps are already known.
opts: True
False
why: Mapping is a diagnostic for where work waits versus progresses, and that picture changes as soon as the flow changes. Repeating it after go-live is how a team confirms the delay actually moved rather than shifting to a new step, which fits the did we get there step of continual improvement.

q: Which two statements about a 'resolve a customer incident' value stream are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: It may draw on several practices, such as service desk, incident management, and change enablement
It is complete when the customer confirms service is restored and they can work again
It must pass through all eight lifecycle activities to qualify as a value stream
It is complete as soon as the technician applies the fix, whatever the customer then experiences
why: A value stream strings together whichever practices and lifecycle activities one scenario needs, and it ends when the consumer actually realizes value, not when an internal step finishes. Few value streams touch all eight activities, and the technician-applies-the-fix option is the near-miss: it describes an output being produced, not the outcome that closes the stream.

q: An MSP's procurement team runs a stream that renews and re-assigns the software licences its support engineers depend on. A new manager wants it reclassified as core, arguing that 'without it, client support would stop'. Which statement is correct?
opts: It stays enabling: it supports other value streams but serves no external customer directly
It becomes core: any stream that core work depends on inherits core status from them
It is neither: licence handling is a management practice rather than a value stream
It becomes core: the licences are ultimately paid for out of external client fees
why: Core versus enabling is decided by whether the stream creates value directly for an external customer, not by how critical it is or who ultimately funds it. Dependency does not transfer core status, and an end-to-end renewal flow spanning several steps and practices is a value stream, not a single practice.

q: Which of the following is the best example of an enabling value stream?
opts: Renewing an internal software license used only by the IT department itself
Resolving a customer-facing support ticket
Delivering a signed contract directly to an external client
Responding to a customer's product inquiry
why: Renewing an internal license never touches the external customer directly, which is exactly what makes it an enabling value stream -- it supports other value streams internally instead. Resolving a ticket, delivering a contract, and responding to an inquiry all involve direct interaction with an external customer, making each of those a core value stream instead.

q: Which of the following describes a value stream, rather than work inside a single management practice?
opts: Logging and categorizing a reported fault at the service desk
Resolving a user's incident from first report to confirmed closure
Assessing and authorizing a normal change at the change advisory board
Diagnosing a suspected network fault within the network team
why: A value stream runs end to end for one scenario, from demand to value realized, and typically crosses several practices on the way: here the service desk, incident management, possibly change enablement, and the user confirming the outcome. The other three are each a step inside one practice (service desk, change enablement, incident management), however important that step is.

q: In a 'fulfil an access request' value stream, the stream is finished once the access team has provisioned the account, even if the user has not yet been told how to log in.
opts: True
False
why: A value stream ends when the consumer actually realizes value, which here means the user can log in and work. Provisioning is an internal step producing an output; until the user knows about it and can use it, the outcome has not occurred and the stream is still open, however complete the internal work looks.

q: Which two of the following describe a value stream, rather than a single practice or a single step within one? (Choose two.)
opts: Taking a new starter from signed offer to a productive first day with laptop, badge, and access
Taking a feature from customer request through build, release, and first use
Change enablement, including its risk-assessment and authorization steps
The approval step in which the change authority signs off a normal change
why: The first two run end to end from a demand to value realized by the consumer, drawing on several practices along the way, which is what a value stream is. Change enablement is a single practice, however many steps it contains, and the authorization step is one activity inside that practice. The practice option is the near-miss: it has internal steps, but it is still one set of resources for one kind of work.

q: A service desk runs three AI tools: (1) one drafts replies that an agent reviews before sending; (2) one reads each new ticket, searches the knowledge base, applies the fix, and closes the ticket with no human step; (3) one flags tickets whose wording suggests a security issue. Which of these is agentic AI?
opts: Tool 2 only
Tools 1 and 2
Tool 1 only
Tools 2 and 3
why: Agentic AI plans and carries out a multi-step task toward a goal with limited human intervention, which only tool 2 does. Tool 1 is generative: it creates content but a human decides what happens next. Tool 3 performs a single classification and takes no further action, so it is AI assisting a human workflow rather than acting autonomously through it.

q: A tooling team rolls out an AI assistant for the service desk without any decision about who is accountable for its recommendations, how its behaviour is monitored, or when it may act without a human. Which Value System component is missing from the rollout?
opts: Governance
Continual improvement
The guiding principles
A management practice
why: Accountability, monitoring, and limits on autonomy are matters of direction and control, which is governance; ITIL treats AI as a capability that needs it like any other. Continual improvement is the near-miss, since monitoring feeds improvement, but the gap described is the absence of direction, not of improvement. The guiding principles are recommendations rather than a control mechanism, and a practice (the tooling team) is clearly already at work.

q: A chatbot writes a complete, well-worded incident summary whenever an agent asks, but does nothing until asked and takes no action on the ticket. A colleague calls it agentic because its output is sophisticated. What is the correct classification?
opts: Generative: it creates content but does not plan or act toward a goal itself
Agentic: producing a full summary involves several reasoning steps
Agentic: it operates inside the ticketing system rather than standalone
Generative: an AI that produces text can never also be agentic
why: The axis that separates the two is autonomous planning and action, not output quality. The chatbot only produces content on request, so it is generative. Sophistication and where the tool runs are irrelevant to the distinction, and the claim that a text-producing AI can never also be agentic reaches the right label for the wrong reason: agentic systems often include generative capabilities, so producing text does not rule agentic out.

q: A support team lets an AI agent auto-resolve simple password resets, but requires human sign-off before any AI action affecting a production server. What does this reflect?
opts: A guiding principle being ignored in favor of pure automation
AI governance applied proportionally to risk
A cautious limitation on agentic AI's scope until trust in it grows
A failure of the value chain to define clear activities
why: This is AI governance in practice — oversight applied in proportion to risk, allowing autonomy for low-risk actions while requiring approval for higher-risk ones.

q: An AI-assisted change process automatically approves low-risk standard changes but routes anything touching a regulated system to a human review board. What does this best describe?
opts: Automation replacing governance for low-risk changes
Standard changes being reclassified as normal changes
An emergency change procedure triggered automatically
AI governance calibrated to risk
why: Letting AI approve pre-authorized low-risk changes while routing anything touching a regulated system to humans is oversight applied in proportion to risk. Automation replacing governance is the near-miss: the auto-approval is itself a governed rule, not an absence of governance. Nothing in the scenario reclassifies change types or invokes the emergency procedure.

q: An AI tool that drafts an entire knowledge article from a resolved ticket, for a human to approve and publish, counts as agentic AI because it produced the whole article unaided.
opts: True
False
why: Producing content, however complete, is generative AI. Agentic AI is defined by planning and acting toward a goal with limited human intervention; here a human still decides whether anything happens with the output, so no autonomous action has taken place.

q: Because a new AI triage assistant only makes suggestions, questions of accountability and monitoring can reasonably be deferred until it is given authority to act on its own.
opts: True
False
why: ITIL treats AI as a capability that needs governance from the start, in proportion to its risk, not only once it acts autonomously. Suggestions still shape human decisions, so someone must be accountable for their quality and bias, and monitoring is what produces the evidence needed before wider authority is granted.

q: An AI tool automatically assigns an incoming incident to the right team and triggers the matching runbook. Which AI capability is this?
opts: Coordination
Curation
Cognition
Clarification
