why: Orchestrating a workflow, like assigning a ticket and kicking off a runbook, is Coordination. Curation organizes or filters information, Cognition makes a decision or prediction, and Clarification explains something in simpler terms.

q: An organization is cataloguing its AI tools against the AI Capability Model. Which two of the following tools are classified correctly? (Choose two.)
opts: A tool that filters thousands of alerts down to the few worth human attention: Curation
A tool that predicts which servers will breach capacity next month: Cognition
A tool that drafts a knowledge article from a resolved ticket: Clarification
A tool that rewrites a technical root-cause note in plain language for users: Creation
why: Filtering and organizing information is Curation, and predicting or deciding is Cognition. The other two are swapped: drafting a new article is Creation (generating content), while rewriting something technical so people understand it is Clarification. The six capabilities are Creation, Curation, Clarification, Cognition, Communication, and Coordination.

q: Which two of the following AI uses are correctly matched to their capability in the AI Capability Model? (Choose two.)
opts: A virtual agent that chats with users to gather incident details: Communication
An orchestrator that sequences the diagnostic, approval, and remediation steps across tools: Coordination
A model that ranks which open incidents are likely to breach their targets: Curation
A tool that condenses a 30-page vendor contract into its key obligations: Cognition
why: Interacting with people is Communication and orchestrating a workflow across tools is Coordination. Ranking incidents by likely breach is a prediction, which is Cognition rather than Curation, and condensing a contract into plain key points is Clarification (or Curation of its content), not Cognition. The six capabilities are Creation, Curation, Clarification, Cognition, Communication, and Coordination.

q: A new HR system is rolled out with a defined start, end, budget, and project board. Once live, it is supported under existing SLAs and improved over time. Which framework fits each phase?
opts: PRINCE2 for the rollout; ITIL for the live service
ITIL for the rollout; PRINCE2 for the live service
PRINCE2 for both, since the project board stays accountable
ITIL for both, since PRINCE2 covers only software projects
why: PRINCE2 manages temporary, bounded work with a defined start and end; ITIL manages the ongoing service that work delivers into. Using ITIL for the rollout and PRINCE2 for the live service reverses the layers, using PRINCE2 for both ignores that the project closes once the system is live, and the claim that PRINCE2 covers only software projects misstates it, since it applies to projects of any kind.

q: A development team works in two-week sprints and demos each increment to users. The operations team asks how this fits with the organization's ITIL adoption. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: Agile shapes how the team delivers iteratively; ITIL frames the wider service value context
They overlap, so sprints should stop wherever an ITIL practice already exists
ITIL applies only after the final sprint, when the product is handed to operations
Agile replaces progress iteratively with feedback, so that principle no longer applies
why: Agile and ITIL sit at different layers: Agile is a way of doing the work in small increments, while ITIL describes the service value system that work contributes to, including the principle that already favours iteration. The claim that ITIL applies only after the final sprint is the near-miss: ITIL is not confined to operations after hand-over, since Discover, Design, and Build are lifecycle activities too. Neither framework displaces the other.

q: A team automates its build, test, and deployment pipeline using DevOps practices and wants ITIL to govern how those releases fit into the wider service value system. Which description of the relationship is most accurate?
opts: DevOps and ITIL solve the same problem, so running both duplicates effort
ITIL provides the value system and governance; DevOps contributes practices for fast, collaborative delivery
DevOps supplies the governance layer; ITIL contributes the delivery pipeline practices
ITIL expects automated pipelines to be replaced by a formal change board
why: ITIL and DevOps operate at different layers: CI/CD practices sit inside the Build, Transition, and Deliver activities, governed by the wider ITIL context. Giving DevOps the governance layer and ITIL the pipeline practices is the reversed near-miss, assigning each framework the other's role. Treating them as substitutes that duplicate effort is wrong, and expecting pipelines to be replaced by a formal change board misreads change enablement, which can be satisfied by pre-authorized standard changes flowing through a pipeline.

q: A rollout team proposes running a new system's deployment as a PRINCE2 project, then handing it to teams working under ITIL practices once live. A manager objects that ITIL does not support mixing frameworks this way. The manager is correct.
opts: True
False
why: This is exactly how the two are meant to fit: PRINCE2 manages the temporary, bounded project, and ITIL manages the ongoing service it delivers into. ITIL positions itself as complementary to project, agile, and DevOps methods rather than as a replacement for them.

q: A CIO learns that ITIL, Agile, DevOps, and PRINCE2 are all 'in use' across her organization and worries they conflict. Which statement best explains how they can coexist?
opts: ITIL supplies the service value system and governance; the others contribute practices for how particular work gets done
Each covers the full service lifecycle, so the organization should standardize on whichever is most mature
ITIL incorporates the other three, so adopting ITIL means the others are already in place
The others apply only to development work, while ITIL applies only to live operations
why: The frameworks sit at different layers: ITIL frames the overall value system, while Agile, DevOps, and PRINCE2 offer specific ways of doing iterative, delivery, and project work inside it. The claim that the others apply only to development while ITIL applies only to live operations is the near-miss, since ITIL also covers Discover, Design, and Build rather than operations alone. ITIL neither absorbs the others nor demands a single-framework choice.

q: A DevOps team that deploys through an automated pipeline is operating outside ITIL change enablement, because ITIL requires every change to be individually approved.
opts: True
False
why: Change enablement classifies changes by risk: a low-risk, well-understood, pre-authorized change is a standard change and needs no case-by-case approval, which is exactly how a tested pipeline deployment can be governed. DevOps practices sit inside the ITIL value system rather than outside it.
